questions.title: OSI vs. TCP/IP: Why Two Models Still Matter
questions.prompt: A junior analyst asks why they need to learn both the OSI model and the TCP/IP model when they describe "basically the same thing." Explain how the two models actually map to each other, and give one concrete reason a SOC analyst benefits from knowing both rather than just one.
questions.modelAnswer: The OSI model has seven layers -- Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application -- while the TCP/IP model has four: Link, Internet, Transport, and Application. They aren't two different descriptions of the same single thing; TCP/IP's Application layer absorbs OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session layers into one, and TCP/IP's Link layer absorbs OSI's Data Link and Physical layers into one. The Transport and Network/Internet layers map cleanly one-to-one between the two models. The practical reason to know both: real tools and vendor documentation constantly use OSI layer numbers as shorthand (a "Layer 7 firewall" inspects application data, a "Layer 3 switch" routes), while TCP/IP is what's actually implemented in the headers you inspect in Wireshark or a packet capture. An analyst who only knows one vocabulary will misunderstand either the vendor's marketing language or the actual packet structure they're staring at.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them OSI is the vocabulary the industry talks in, and TCP/IP is what's actually running on the wire -- you need both, not because they disagree, but because they're used for different jobs. When someone says a firewall does "Layer 7 inspection" or a load balancer works at "Layer 4," that's OSI language, and if you don't have those seven layers memorized, that sentence means nothing to you even though you understand networking fine otherwise. But when I'm actually looking at a packet capture, I'm thinking in TCP/IP's four layers, because that's what the headers in front of me actually implement. I usually draw the mapping once for a new analyst: Application/Presentation/Session all collapse into TCP/IP's Application layer, Data Link and Physical collapse into TCP/IP's Link layer, and Transport and Network line up directly. Once that's visual, the "why do I need both" question answers itself.
commonMistakes: Assuming the two models have a clean one-to-one layer mapping instead of several-to-one in places
Thinking TCP/IP's Application layer has no equivalent to OSI's Session or Presentation layers, when it actually absorbs both
Dismissing OSI as "purely theoretical" and therefore not worth learning, when vendor and tool documentation uses it constantly
keyPoints: OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP has four
TCP/IP's Application layer absorbs OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session layers
TCP/IP's Link layer absorbs OSI's Data Link and Physical layers
Vendor/tool language (Layer 3, Layer 7) uses OSI numbering even when the actual implementation is TCP/IP

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states OSI's seven layers
Correctly states TCP/IP's four layers and how they map to OSI
Gives a genuine practical reason for knowing both
Clear, accurate explanation overall

questions.title: The CIA Triad in a Real Tradeoff
questions.prompt: Explain the CIA triad, and then walk through a real example where improving one leg of the triad -- say, Availability -- can directly work against another leg, like Confidentiality. Use a concrete scenario.
questions.modelAnswer: The CIA triad names the three properties security is built to protect: Confidentiality (only authorized people can read the data), Integrity (data isn't modified by anyone unauthorized), and Availability (authorized people can actually access the data and systems when they need to). These three properties are frequently in tension, not automatically aligned. A concrete example: to improve Availability, a team stands up a hot failover database replica in a second region so the application survives a regional outage. If that replica isn't hardened and monitored to the same standard as the primary -- same access controls, same encryption, same patching cadence -- it becomes a second, weaker attack surface holding the exact same sensitive data, directly undermining Confidentiality. The fix isn't to avoid the failover; it's to recognize that an Availability improvement created a new Confidentiality obligation that has to be engineered for explicitly, not assumed to come along for free.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always push back a little when someone treats CIA like three boxes to check independently, because in practice they pull against each other constantly, and that tension is exactly what a security engineer gets paid to navigate. The example I give is a failover replica: the business wants five-nines uptime, so you stand up a hot standby in another region. Great for Availability. But now you've doubled your attack surface for the same sensitive data, and if nobody explicitly re-applies the same access controls and monitoring to that replica, you've quietly traded away some Confidentiality to get that Availability win. I've also seen the reverse -- a team locks down access so tightly after an audit finding that the on-call engineer can't actually get into a system during a real outage, which trades Availability for Confidentiality. The point isn't that one property should always win; it's that every control you add should be evaluated against all three, not just the one it was designed to fix.
commonMistakes: Treating the CIA triad as three independent goals with no tension between them
Confusing Integrity with correctness or accuracy rather than unauthorized modification specifically
Assuming any new security control automatically improves all three properties at once
keyPoints: Correct definitions of Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability
A concrete scenario where improving one property genuinely works against another
Recognition that the tradeoff has to be engineered for, not ignored

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three legs of the triad
Explains the tradeoff mechanism clearly and correctly
Uses a concrete, believable scenario rather than an abstract one

questions.title: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Encryption: Where Each One Actually Gets Used
questions.prompt: Explain the core difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, and then explain why TLS uses both together instead of picking just one.
questions.modelAnswer: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting -- it's fast and efficient, but it has a key-distribution problem: both parties need the same secret key, and getting that key to the other party securely in the first place is hard. Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair, a public key anyone can have and a private key only the owner holds; data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key. This solves the distribution problem -- the public key can be shared openly -- but asymmetric operations are computationally expensive and far slower than symmetric ones at scale. TLS uses both because each solves the other's weakness: during the handshake, asymmetric cryptography (or a key-exchange mechanism built on the same public/private key math) is used just once to securely establish a shared secret between client and server, and then that shared secret becomes a symmetric session key used to encrypt the actual bulk data for the rest of the connection, fast.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd walk someone through it: symmetric is fast but has a 'how do I hand you the key safely' problem, and asymmetric solves that handoff problem but is too slow to use for actually encrypting a whole web session's worth of data. TLS doesn't pick a side -- it uses asymmetric crypto for exactly the part it's good at, the handshake where client and server agree on a secret without ever transmitting that secret in the clear, and then switches to a symmetric session key for everything after that, because symmetric is cheap enough to encrypt megabytes of traffic without grinding your CPU to a halt. If someone tells me HTTPS 'uses asymmetric encryption' as the whole answer, that's the tell they haven't actually looked at what happens after the handshake completes.
commonMistakes: Saying asymmetric encryption is simply "more secure" rather than solving a different problem (key distribution) than symmetric
Believing HTTPS/TLS encrypts the entire session using only asymmetric encryption
Confusing the key-exchange step with the algorithm used to encrypt the actual data afterward
keyPoints: Symmetric: one shared key, fast, has a key-distribution problem
Asymmetric: public/private key pair, solves distribution, computationally expensive
TLS handshake uses asymmetric/key-exchange crypto once to establish a shared secret
The rest of the session uses that shared secret as a fast symmetric key

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines symmetric encryption and its weakness
Correctly defines asymmetric encryption and its tradeoff
Correctly explains the hybrid model TLS actually uses
Avoids the common "HTTPS is just asymmetric" misconception

lessonLink.label: Review: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Encryption

questions.title: Hashing vs. Encryption, and What a Digital Signature Actually Proves
questions.prompt: A teammate says "we hash passwords to encrypt them." Correct this statement, and explain what a digital signature actually proves that a plain hash alone does not.
questions.modelAnswer: That statement conflates two different operations. Hashing is one-way -- it's not reversible the way encryption is, and there's no decryption key that turns a hash back into the original password. The reason passwords are hashed instead of encrypted is specifically so the plaintext is never stored anywhere, even by the system that needs to verify it: at login, the system hashes the entered password again and compares the two hashes, never needing to recover the original. A digital signature is a different mechanism built on top of hashing: the sender hashes a message, then encrypts that hash with their own private key. Anyone with the sender's public key can decrypt that signature back into the original hash value, independently hash the message themselves, and compare the two. If they match, it proves two things a plain hash alone cannot: Integrity (the message wasn't altered after signing) and Authenticity/non-repudiation (it really came from whoever holds that private key, not just whoever happened to be on the wire).
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd fix is the word "encrypt" -- hashing isn't encryption, and the whole reason we hash a password instead of encrypting it is that we never want anyone, including us, to be able to reverse it back to plaintext. If someone says "we can decrypt the hash to check it," that's the sign they don't actually understand what's happening at login -- we hash the attempt and compare hashes, full stop. For the signature question, I like to point out that a plain hash by itself proves nothing about who sent something -- it only proves the data matches whatever it's being compared against, and that comparison is only as trustworthy as the channel it came over. A digital signature adds the sender's private key into the mix, so verifying it proves the message came from that specific key holder and wasn't tampered with afterward -- that's authenticity and integrity together, which a bare hash was never designed to provide on its own.
commonMistakes: Calling hashing "encryption" or implying a hash can be reversed with the right tool or key
Believing a plain hash alone proves who sent a message, not just that the data matches
Confusing the signing key (private key of the sender) with the verification key (their public key)
keyPoints: Hashing is one-way and not reversible, unlike encryption
A digital signature = hash of a message encrypted with the sender's private key
Verifying it (with the sender's public key) proves both integrity and authenticity
A plain hash alone only proves data matches a comparison, not who produced it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes hashing from encryption
Correctly explains the digital signature mechanism
Correctly explains what a signature adds over a plain hash

questions.title: Kill Chain vs. MITRE ATT&CK: Two Tools, Two Jobs
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain and the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and explain why a SOC analyst triaging a real incident typically references both rather than picking just one.
questions.modelAnswer: The Cyber Kill Chain is a simple, linear, seven-stage narrative of how a typical intrusion progresses -- Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command & Control, and Actions on Objectives -- and its value is that breaking any single link anywhere in that chain stops the whole attack from reaching its goal. MITRE ATT&CK is a completely different kind of resource: a free, continuously updated, non-linear knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics (the attacker's goal at a given moment, like Persistence or Lateral Movement) and techniques (the specific, numbered method used to achieve that goal), built from actually documented intrusions. An analyst triaging a real incident uses the kill chain to answer "where are we in this attack and how far have they gotten" -- useful for deciding urgency and what to stop first -- and then uses ATT&CK to answer "exactly which technique did they use here, and what else does this specific adversary group typically pair it with" -- useful for writing the precise detection rule or closing the specific gap that let it happen. The kill chain gives the narrative; ATT&CK gives the technical precision.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the kill chain as the story I'd tell a non-technical stakeholder about what happened, and ATT&CK as the technical reference I actually work from while I'm triaging. If I tell someone "the attacker got as far as installing persistent malware before we caught it," that's kill-chain language and it communicates urgency clearly. But when I'm actually writing up the incident or building a new detection, I need the ATT&CK technique ID -- something like T1059 for a scripting interpreter -- because that's the vocabulary that lets another analyst, or a vendor's threat report, or next year's me, know exactly what happened without ambiguity. I use both in the same incident, just for different audiences and different purposes -- I wouldn't try to replace one with the other.
commonMistakes: Treating MITRE ATT&CK as a replacement for the kill chain instead of a complementary, more granular tool
Assuming a real attack must pass through every kill-chain stage in strict order with no stages skipped or combined
Confusing an ATT&CK tactic (the goal) with a technique (the specific method used to achieve it)
keyPoints: Kill chain: seven linear stages describing an intrusion's overall arc
ATT&CK: a non-linear catalog of real-world tactics and techniques, each with a stable ID
Kill chain answers "how far did they get"; ATT&CK answers "exactly what did they do"
Breaking the chain at any single stage counts as a full defensive success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the kill chain's structure and purpose
Correctly describes ATT&CK, including tactic vs. technique
Correctly reasons why an analyst would use both together
Gives an accurate, concrete example of each in use

questions.title: Stateful vs. Stateless Firewalls: What the State Table Buys You
questions.prompt: Explain what a firewall's state table actually does, and why nearly every production firewall today is stateful rather than stateless. Then explain one place where stateless filtering still has a legitimate role.
questions.modelAnswer: A stateful firewall maintains a state table -- a running record of every active connection passing through it, including who opened it and what reply traffic is expected back. When an internal host opens a connection out, the firewall logs it; when the matching reply arrives, the firewall checks it against the table, recognizes it as part of a connection the internal host itself initiated, and lets it through automatically, with no separate inbound rule needed. A stateless firewall has no such memory -- every packet is judged independently against static rules (source, destination, port, protocol), so an administrator has to write an explicit rule permitting reply traffic, which is both tedious and error-prone. Nearly every modern firewall is stateful because understanding connections, not just individual packets, is a real security benefit that modern hardware can easily afford the CPU and memory cost for. Stateless filtering still earns its place on resource-constrained devices, or as a cheap, fast first filtering pass (like a router access control list doing simple traffic shaping) before traffic reaches a stateful device that does the real connection-aware inspection.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I explain the state table to someone new is: it's the firewall's memory of 'who asked for what.' Without it, the firewall has amnesia -- every single packet, including a reply to a connection the firewall itself just watched get opened two seconds ago, gets judged completely from scratch against a static rule list. That's why stateless rule sets are such a pain to write correctly -- you either end up opening a wide port range just to catch replies, which is too permissive, or you miss a legitimate return path, which breaks something. Almost everything I touch day to day is stateful because the hardware cost of tracking connections just isn't the constraint it used to be. Where I've actually seen stateless filtering still matter is as a cheap first-pass ACL on a router, filtering out obviously bad traffic before it ever reaches the stateful firewall doing the real work -- cheap and dumb, but that's fine for a first pass.
commonMistakes: Believing a stateless firewall can't filter by port or protocol at all (it can -- it just has no memory of connections)
Thinking "stateful" just means "smarter rule-writing" rather than specifically connection tracking
Assuming stateless firewalls are obsolete and never legitimately used anymore
keyPoints: State table: tracks active connections, auto-permits matching reply traffic
Stateless: judges every packet independently, needs explicit rules for replies
Tradeoff: stateful is smarter but costs CPU/memory; stateless is cheap but dumb
Stateless filtering still has a role as a cheap first pass or on constrained hardware

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what the state table does
Correctly explains the real tradeoff between the two
Correctly identifies a legitimate current use for stateless filtering
Clear and accurate overall

questions.title: IDS vs. IPS: The Tradeoff Behind "Can It Block"
questions.prompt: Explain the structural difference between an IDS and an IPS (not just "detect vs. prevent"), and explain the real risk an IPS introduces that an IDS never can.
questions.modelAnswer: An IDS is a passive sensor: a switch sends it a copy of the traffic, usually through a SPAN port or a network tap, and the IDS inspects that copy and raises an alert when something matches. Because it only ever sees a copy, it has no physical ability to stop the traffic it just flagged -- by the time it sees the packet, the original has already reached its destination. An IPS runs similar detection logic, but it's deployed inline, directly in the traffic's actual path, the same way a firewall is; every packet has to pass through it, so when it matches something malicious, it can drop the packet, reset the connection, or block the source in real time. The real risk that comes with that inline position: a false positive on an IPS isn't just a noisy alert, it's a real outage, because blocking legitimate traffic by mistake takes down whatever business process depended on it. An IDS can never cause that kind of outage, because it never touches the live packet -- but it also can never stop an attack already underway.
questions.professionalAnswer: People often say "IDS detects, IPS prevents" and leave it there, but the part that actually matters operationally is where each one physically sits. An IDS is looking at a mirrored copy of traffic -- it's a bystander, not a gatekeeper, so whatever it decides about a packet, that packet already arrived wherever it was going. An IPS sits directly in the road the traffic has to travel through, which is the only reason it's physically capable of dropping or resetting a connection. The tradeoff I actually weigh when deciding deployment mode is: how confident am I in this rule's false-positive rate, because if I'm wrong and this is an IPS, I just took down a real business process, not just generated a noisy ticket. That's exactly why a new rule earns its way into blocking mode instead of starting there.
commonMistakes: Treating IDS vs. IPS as a pure software setting rather than a real architectural difference in where the sensor sits
Assuming IPS is strictly "better" than IDS because it can block, without weighing the outage risk
Forgetting that a new detection rule is typically run in passive/alert-only mode first to measure its false-positive rate before trusting it to block
keyPoints: IDS: passive, sees a copy of traffic via SPAN/tap, can only alert
IPS: inline, sees the actual traffic, can drop/reset/block in real time
IPS false positive = real outage; IDS false positive = noisy alert, nothing more
New rules are commonly deployed in IDS/alert-only mode before being trusted to block

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the physical/architectural deployment difference
Correctly describes what each one can actually do on a match
Correctly explains the real risk IPS introduces
Mentions the staged IDS-before-IPS deployment practice

lessonLink.label: Review: IDS vs. IPS

questions.title: The NIST Incident Response Lifecycle Is a Loop, Not a Line
questions.prompt: Name the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle in order, and explain why it's drawn as a cycle rather than a straight line -- specifically, what does Post-Incident Activity actually feed back into?
questions.modelAnswer: The four phases, in order, are Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity. It's drawn as a cycle, with an arrow running from Post-Incident Activity back to Preparation, because every real incident teaches a team something it didn't already know -- a gap in the IR plan, a log source that wasn't actually feeding the SIEM, a backup-restore process nobody had tested in a year. Post-Incident Activity is the lessons-learned review where those gaps get identified and written down, and feeding them back into Preparation is exactly what makes the next incident go faster and cleaner than this one did. A team that treats Post-Incident Activity as optional paperwork is a team that keeps relearning the same lessons live, during the worst possible time to be learning them.
questions.professionalAnswer: If I'm asked to name the four phases, I go Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, Post-Incident Activity -- and I always emphasize that third one is really three related things bundled together, not one monolithic step. But the part I actually think matters more in an interview is explaining why NIST drew an arrow back to the start instead of ending the diagram at Post-Incident Activity. Every incident I've been part of surfaced at least one thing that wasn't in the plan -- maybe nobody had clearly documented who has authority to pull a production server offline at 2 a.m. That finding is worthless if it just sits in a report; it has to go back into Preparation as an actual plan update, a new tabletop scenario, a filled gap -- otherwise you're not actually improving, you're just writing the same postmortem again next time.
commonMistakes: Naming only three phases, or merging Containment, Eradication, and Recovery into one step without being able to separate them when asked
Treating Post-Incident Activity as optional paperwork rather than the mechanism that improves future response
Assuming the lifecycle ends after Recovery instead of looping back into Preparation
keyPoints: Correct four phases in order: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, Post-Incident Activity
The cycle shape exists because every incident reveals a gap worth fixing
Post-Incident Activity's findings feed directly back into Preparation
A concrete example of a gap found and fixed strengthens the answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names all four phases in order
Correctly explains the cycle shape and the feedback into Preparation
Gives or recognizes a concrete example of this feedback loop
Clear and accurate overall

questions.title: RBAC vs. ABAC: When a Role Isn't Enough
questions.prompt: Explain the core difference between role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC), and describe a real access requirement that RBAC alone struggles to express cleanly but ABAC handles naturally.
questions.modelAnswer: RBAC assigns permissions through a named role tied to a job function -- a user is a member of "Tier-1 Support" or "AP Clerk," and that role carries a fixed set of permissions. ABAC instead evaluates a policy at request time against attributes of the subject, the resource, and the environment together -- for example, "allow if the user's department matches the resource's department, AND the request happens during business hours, AND the device is compliant." A real requirement RBAC struggles with: access that should depend on context rather than job title, like a support rep who can view a customer record only when it belongs to their own region and only from a managed device. Expressing that purely through roles invites exactly the role-explosion failure mode -- "Support-Tier1-EastRegion-CompliantDevice" as its own role -- because every new combination of conditions demands a new near-duplicate role. ABAC expresses the same requirement as a single policy with multiple attribute conditions, with no new role required.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't frame this as ABAC replacing RBAC -- most mature organizations run both, RBAC for the baseline "what does this job function need" and ABAC layered on top for context-sensitive decisions. The example I always reach for is region- or device-dependent access: if a support rep's access should only apply to their own region and only from a company-managed laptop, RBAC alone forces you into naming a role for every combination of region times device state times whatever else comes up next, and that's exactly the role-explosion trap -- dozens of nearly identical roles nobody can audit. ABAC just writes that as attribute conditions evaluated at request time, with zero new roles created. The tell that an org actually needs ABAC, not just "better RBAC," is when you notice yourself creating a new role for every small contextual variation instead of reusing the same base role.
commonMistakes: Implying ABAC replaces RBAC everywhere, when most real environments combine both
Confusing an ABAC attribute with simple group membership rather than a dynamically evaluated condition
Describing the RBAC weakness in the abstract without tying it back to the specific role-explosion failure mode it causes
keyPoints: RBAC: permissions tied to a named role representing a job function
ABAC: policy evaluated against subject/resource/environment attributes at request time
A concrete context-dependent requirement (region, device compliance, time) that RBAC alone handles poorly
The connection to role explosion as the specific symptom of RBAC's limit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines RBAC
Correctly defines ABAC
Gives a concrete, well-reasoned example requirement
Explicitly ties the RBAC weakness to role explosion

lessonLink.label: Review: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

questions.title: Platform-Managed vs. Customer-Managed Encryption Keys
questions.prompt: Both Azure and AWS encrypt data at rest by default. Explain what actually differs between a platform-managed key and a customer-managed key (CMK), and when CMK is worth its operational overhead versus when it's not.
questions.modelAnswer: With a platform-managed key, the cloud provider generates, stores, and rotates the encryption key entirely inside its own infrastructure -- you never see it, never touch it, and can't revoke access to it independently of deleting the resource itself. With a customer-managed key, you create and own the key in Azure Key Vault or AWS KMS, and the storage or database service calls out to that vault to perform the actual encrypt/decrypt operations; you control the key's access policy and rotation schedule, and critically, you can revoke access to the key, which instantly makes the encrypted data unreadable even though the ciphertext itself never moves. The difference isn't encryption strength -- both models use the same strong encryption underneath. CMK is worth the operational overhead when a compliance framework or customer contract explicitly requires independent, customer-controlled revocation, when you need a detailed audit trail of every key operation, or when you need a guaranteed "kill switch" during an offboarding or suspected breach. Outside those specific drivers, a platform-managed key is not a lesser security posture -- it's the same encryption, managed by a team whose entire job is rotating and protecting keys correctly, with none of the rotation-policy and access-policy maintenance burden CMK adds.
questions.professionalAnswer: The question I ask whenever someone proposes switching to customer-managed keys "for security" is: what specific capability do you actually need that you don't have today? Because the encryption itself isn't stronger with CMK -- it's the exact same algorithm either way. What CMK actually buys you is a kill switch: the ability to instantly make data unreadable by revoking access to the key, independent of deleting the storage resource, plus your own detailed log of every time that key was used. If a compliance framework or a customer contract specifically demands that kind of independent control, CMK earns its overhead. If nobody can point to that requirement, I push back on adding CMK, because now you own key rotation policies, access policies to audit, and a brand-new single point of failure if that key becomes inaccessible -- real operational cost for a security property nobody actually asked for.
commonMistakes: Claiming CMK is "stronger encryption" rather than the same encryption with different key control
Treating CMK as always the right default choice regardless of an actual compliance or contractual driver
Forgetting CMK requires its own ongoing rotation-policy and access-policy maintenance
keyPoints: Platform-managed key: provider-controlled, no independent revoke capability
Customer-managed key: customer-controlled, revocable independently, auditable key operations
Neither is "stronger" encryption -- the difference is control, not algorithm strength
CMK is justified by a real compliance/audit/revocation requirement, not by default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines both key models
Correctly explains the "kill switch"/revocation capability CMK adds
Gives correct judgment on when CMK is and isn't justified
Clarity

lessonLink.label: Review: Encryption at Rest and in Transit

questions.title: SAST vs. Dependency Scanning: Two Different Blind Spots
questions.prompt: Explain what SAST actually checks versus what dependency scanning (SCA) checks, and explain why a project can pass a clean SAST scan and still ship a serious vulnerability.
questions.modelAnswer: SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your own source code -- not a running application -- and looks for known-dangerous patterns: string-built SQL queries vulnerable to injection, weak cryptographic functions, hardcoded secrets, unsanitized input flowing into a shell command. Because it never executes the application, it can run in seconds against just a pull request's diff. Dependency scanning, or software composition analysis (SCA), checks something SAST never looks at: the exact versions of third-party packages your project imports but never wrote, comparing those pinned versions against public vulnerability databases. A project can have flawless code of its own -- a perfectly clean SAST scan -- and still ship a serious vulnerability simply by depending on a library version with a disclosed, known issue, because that vulnerability lives in code SAST was never scanning in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as two completely different blind spots covered by two different tools. SAST is looking at the code your team actually wrote, line by line, for dangerous patterns -- think Bandit for Python or Semgrep across languages. Dependency scanning is looking at everything your project pulls in that your team never wrote a line of -- think pip-audit against the Python Packaging Advisory Database, or npm audit for Node. The reason you need both and not just one: I've seen a team ship genuinely clean, careful code and still have a real incident because a pinned version of a logging library had a disclosed remote-code-execution bug that their own SAST scan was never looking at, because SAST only ever looks at the code the team itself wrote. Neither tool requires running the app, which is exactly why both run cheaply on every pull request instead of waiting for a later, slower stage.
commonMistakes: Assuming SAST also covers third-party libraries, when it only looks at your own source
Assuming either tool requires the application to actually be running (neither does)
Treating every SAST or SCA finding as an automatic hard blocker instead of triaging real risk
keyPoints: SAST: analyzes your own source code for dangerous patterns, without executing it
SCA/dependency scanning: checks third-party package versions against known-vulnerability databases
A clean SAST scan says nothing about a vulnerable dependency version
Naming at least one real tool for each (e.g., Bandit, pip-audit)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines SAST
Correctly defines SCA/dependency scanning
Correctly explains the specific blind-spot scenario
References at least one real tool accurately

questions.title: Credential Vaulting vs. Session Recording: What Each One Actually Controls
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between credential vaulting and session recording in a PAM program, and why a mature program needs both rather than treating vaulting alone as "done."
questions.modelAnswer: A standing privileged account -- one that holds elevated rights all the time, whether or not anyone is actively using that privilege right now -- is a maximum-value target for every attacker on the network, because it never needs to wait for the right moment to be useful. Credential vaulting addresses who can obtain that privilege: privileged passwords are stored in an encrypted vault instead of memorized or shared, and an admin checks a credential out when they need it, often with automatic rotation afterward so the password can't be reused outside the vault. But vaulting alone only answers who got the credential and when -- it doesn't capture what they actually did with it once checked out. Session recording closes that gap by capturing the commands run and the screen activity during the privileged session itself, turning "we think the account was used for something" into an exact, reviewable record. A program with vaulting but no session recording has controlled access but has no real visibility into privileged activity, which is exactly the gap that matters most during an actual incident review.
questions.professionalAnswer: If someone tells me their PAM program is "done" because they rolled out vaulting, I ask what happens when an admin's vaulted session is later suspected of doing something it shouldn't have. Vaulting tells you who checked the credential out and when -- that's real progress over a shared password nobody could attribute to anyone. But it doesn't tell you what actually happened during that session, and that's exactly the detail you need during incident response. Session recording is what turns a vague "we think this admin account was involved" into an exact command-by-command record you can actually review. I treat vaulting and session recording as two halves of the same control, not sequential maturity steps where one comes "later" -- a program that only has one half has a real, specific gap.
commonMistakes: Believing vaulting alone fully solves the standing-privilege risk without session recording
Confusing session recording with ordinary login/audit logging rather than full command/screen capture
Not recognizing why a standing privileged account is risky even if it's never actually misused
keyPoints: Standing privileged access is a risk independent of whether it's ever misused
Vaulting controls who obtains the credential, with rotation after checkout
Session recording captures what happened during the session itself
A mature program needs both together, not one as a substitute for the other

questions.title: The NIST Zero Trust Tenets Aren't a Shopping List
questions.prompt: A manager says "we bought a ZTNA gateway, so we're zero trust now." Using at least three of the NIST SP 800-207 tenets, explain why that statement is incomplete.
questions.modelAnswer: NIST SP 800-207 defines Zero Trust Architecture as a set of seven tenets -- architectural requirements, not products to buy. Take three: Tenet 3 says access to a resource is granted on a per-session basis, not carried forward automatically; a gateway alone doesn't guarantee every session is independently evaluated rather than relying on a long-lived trust decision. Tenet 4 says access is determined by dynamic policy evaluated from identity, device state, and behavioral/environmental signals together; a gateway that only checks "did this connection come through me" isn't evaluating that combined context unless it's wired into an identity provider and device-compliance signal that actually does. Tenet 5 says the organization continuously monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of every asset; a gateway deployed once and left alone doesn't satisfy "continuously," since posture drifts over time. A ZTNA gateway is one enforcement point that can help satisfy parts of these tenets, but "we bought it" says nothing about whether the dynamic-policy and continuous-monitoring pieces behind it are actually built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently but specifically, because "we bought a ZTNA gateway" is an answer about a purchase, and zero trust is a claim about an architecture's behavior. I'd pick a tenet they can't wave away -- continuous monitoring of asset posture is a good one -- and ask directly: does the gateway, or anything behind it, re-check device compliance after the initial connection, or does a device that passed once stay trusted indefinitely? If the honest answer is "it only checks at connection time," that's a concrete gap against a concrete tenet, not an abstract criticism. NIST deliberately wrote these as requirements a mature architecture satisfies using whatever combination of tools gets there -- so the right response to "we bought the gateway" is never "great, we're done," it's "good, now which of the seven tenets does that actually move us closer to, and which ones still need something else."
commonMistakes: Naming only one tenet and treating that as sufficient to make the point
Treating "zero trust" as a single purchasable product category rather than an architecture
Forgetting the continuous-monitoring tenet specifically, which is where a one-time deployment most visibly falls short
keyPoints: Tenets are architectural requirements, not products
At least three tenets correctly named and explained
A specific explanation of why a gateway alone doesn't satisfy dynamic policy or continuous monitoring
Recognition that a tool can help satisfy a tenet without fully satisfying it alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names and explains three or more tenets
Clearly explains why a single product doesn't satisfy them alone
Clarity and accuracy overall

questions.title: Write a KQL Detection Rule for Brute-Force-Then-Success
questions.prompt: Using Microsoft Sentinel's SigninLogs table (ResultType == "0" for success, non-zero for failure), write a KQL query that flags any UserPrincipalName with more than 5 failed sign-ins in a 10-minute window, followed by a successful sign-in within 10 minutes after that failure cluster. The query must be sequence-aware -- a simple failure count by itself is not enough.
questions.modelAnswer: A simple failure-count query only answers 'did this user have a lot of failures,' not 'did a success follow those failures,' so it fires on both a real brute-force-then-success pattern and an unrelated mix of failures and successes. The correct approach builds two named sub-queries with 'let': one that buckets failed sign-ins into 10-minute bins per user and keeps only buckets with more than 5 failures, capturing the time of the last failure in each bucket; and one that captures every successful sign-in with its timestamp. An inner join on UserPrincipalName lines up each flagged failure cluster with that same user's successes, and a final 'where' clause keeps only the rows where the success landed after the last failure and within a reasonable window afterward -- that final filter is what makes the query sequence-aware instead of just a count.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I see most often is stopping at the failure-count query and calling it done -- it compiles, it returns rows, but it isn't actually answering the question asked. I build this in two clear pieces using 'let' so it reads top to bottom: first, bucket and count failures per user with bin(), filtering to clusters over the threshold and capturing the last failure's timestamp; second, pull every success with its own timestamp. Then I join those two on the user and add the one line that actually matters -- SuccessTime has to be after LastFailure and within the window -- because without that line, the join just pairs every flagged user with every success they've ever had, which isn't a brute-force signal at all.
questions.example:
let Failures = SigninLogs
    | where ResultType != "0"
    | summarize FailedCount = count(), LastFailure = max(TimeGenerated)
        by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
    | where FailedCount > 5;
let Successes = SigninLogs
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
Failures
| join kind=inner Successes on UserPrincipalName
| where SuccessTime > LastFailure and SuccessTime < LastFailure + 10m
| project UserPrincipalName, FailedCount, LastFailure, SuccessTime, IPAddress
commonMistakes: Writing only the failure-count query and treating it as complete, without checking for a subsequent success
Forgetting bin() when bucketing TimeGenerated, leaving failures ungrouped by time window
Joining on UserPrincipalName without constraining SuccessTime to land after LastFailure, which pairs every success with every flagged cluster regardless of timing
Misnaming or forgetting to alias the aggregated columns inside summarize, breaking the later where/join references
keyPoints: summarize + bin() builds the per-user, per-window failure cluster
A separate sub-query captures successful sign-ins with their own timestamp
join kind=inner on UserPrincipalName lines up each user's failures and successes
The final where clause enforcing SuccessTime after LastFailure is what makes it sequence-aware
This finished query is exactly what plugs into a Scheduled Analytics Rule's logic tab

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct failure-count/bin logic with the right threshold
Correct join approach combining failures and successes
Correct time-window constraint that makes the query sequence-aware
Syntactically valid, runnable KQL

questions.title: Write a sudoers Grant for an Automation Account
questions.prompt: A CI/CD deploy script needs to restart the nginx service as root with no human present to type a password, and nothing else. Write the sudoers entry (as it would appear in a file under /etc/sudoers.d/) that grants exactly this, and explain why you'd put it there instead of editing /etc/sudoers directly.
questions.modelAnswer: The entry follows the who where=(as whom) what shape: the deployer account, on ALL hosts, running as root, limited to exactly one absolute-path command, with NOPASSWD so the unattended script isn't blocked waiting for a password prompt that will never come. It belongs in its own file under /etc/sudoers.d/, created and edited with 'sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/90-deployer', rather than in /etc/sudoers directly, for two reasons: the main file is included by default and shouldn't be hand-edited for every one-off grant, and visudo validates syntax before saving so a typo can never leave the live file in a state that locks out sudo for everyone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always write the command as an absolute path, /usr/bin/systemctl, never just systemctl, because sudo deliberately refuses to trust $PATH for a privileged command -- if I left it bare, an attacker could drop a malicious binary named systemctl earlier in some user's path and have it silently run as root instead of the real one. NOPASSWD only goes on this line because it's a non-interactive automation account; I wouldn't put it on a real human's sudo grant, since that removes the one check limiting what a stolen interactive session can do. And I keep this in its own file in sudoers.d rather than editing the shared file directly, so I can see exactly what this one grant is, and remove it later without touching anyone else's access.
questions.example:
# /etc/sudoers.d/90-deployer  (created via: sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/90-deployer)
deployer  ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
commonMistakes: Writing the command as a bare name instead of an absolute path, which sudo won't trust and which opens a PATH-hijacking risk
Granting ALL=(ALL) ALL out of convenience instead of scoping to the one command actually needed
Editing /etc/sudoers directly with a plain text editor instead of visudo, risking a syntax error that locks out sudo entirely
Using NOPASSWD on an interactive human account rather than reserving it for unattended automation
keyPoints: who where=(as whom) what structure of a sudoers line
Absolute path requirement and the PATH-hijacking risk it prevents
NOPASSWD is appropriate here because this is a non-interactive automation account
visudo validates syntax before saving; sudoers.d keeps grants modular

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, properly scoped sudoers grant
Correctly explains the absolute-path requirement and why
Correctly explains visudo/sudoers.d reasoning
Correctly justifies NOPASSWD for this specific account type

questions.title: Write a Detection Rule for a SQL Injection Attempt
questions.prompt: Write a Snort/Suricata rule that alerts (does not block) on any TCP traffic headed to your web servers on port 80 containing the literal string 'UNION SELECT' in the payload. Use a locally-scoped sid, and explain what each field in your rule does.
questions.modelAnswer: The rule follows the standard skeleton: action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options). The action is 'alert,' since blocking wasn't requested; protocol is 'tcp'; the source is 'any any' since the attacker's address and port aren't known in advance; the direction operator points at '$HOME_NET 80,' the variable representing the protected web servers on port 80. Inside the parentheses, msg gives the human-readable description an analyst sees first when triaging; content is the exact byte pattern to match in the payload, here the literal string 'UNION SELECT'; sid is a unique numeric ID, and because this is a locally written rule it should start at 1000000 or above to avoid colliding with an official rule set's IDs; rev tracks the rule's own revision number.
questions.professionalAnswer: I read this rule left to right the same way I'd explain it to someone else: 'alert' means we're only raising a flag, not dropping anything; 'tcp any any' means we don't care what source is sending this, because an attacker's address is never going to be predictable ahead of time; the arrow points at $HOME_NET port 80, so this only fires on traffic headed to our own web servers; and then the content match is the actual signature -- the literal bytes 'UNION SELECT' showing up in a request is a classic SQL injection tell. The two fields I always double check on a new local rule are the sid, which I always start above 1000000 specifically so it can never collide with the official Snort or Suricata rule set's own numbering, and the action, because it's an easy typo to write 'drop' when the requirement was explicitly 'alert only.'
questions.example: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80 (msg:"Possible SQL Injection Attempt"; content:"UNION SELECT"; sid:1000001; rev:1;)
commonMistakes: Writing 'drop' or 'reject' instead of 'alert' when the prompt specifically asked for alert-only behavior
Using a sid inside the official rule set's numbering range instead of the locally-reserved 1000000+ convention
Pointing the direction operator the wrong way, watching traffic leaving $HOME_NET instead of arriving at it
Omitting msg, leaving the alert with no human-readable context for the analyst who triages it
keyPoints: action/protocol/src->dst fields and what each controls
$HOME_NET as the variable representing the protected network
content as the exact payload byte-pattern match
sid numbering convention (1000000+ for local rules) and rev for version tracking

Correct content match syntax for the SQLi pattern
Correct sid numbering convention

questions.title: Write a fail2ban Jail for SSH With Custom Thresholds
questions.prompt: Write the /etc/fail2ban/jail.local stanza that enables SSH brute-force protection on an Ubuntu server, banning an IP for 2 hours after 4 failed attempts within a 5-minute window. Then give the exact command to check that jail's current ban list, and the command to unban an IP that was caught by mistake.
questions.modelAnswer: The stanza goes in jail.local, not jail.conf, because jail.local overrides the shipped defaults and survives a package upgrade. On Ubuntu, the sshd jail's logpath is /var/log/auth.log (RHEL/CentOS would use /var/log/secure instead). maxretry=4 sets the failure count that triggers a ban, findtime=5m is the window those failures have to occur within, and bantime=2h is how long the ban lasts. To check the jail's current state, 'fail2ban-client status sshd' lists its active bans; to remove a specific ban immediately, 'fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip <ip>' takes that IP out of the ban list right away rather than waiting for bantime to expire on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always put this in jail.local and never touch jail.conf directly, because jail.conf is the package's shipped defaults and gets overwritten on the next update -- any edit there just disappears. For the values themselves, I map the prompt straight onto the three settings fail2ban actually cares about: maxretry is the failure count, findtime is the window those failures have to land in, and bantime is how long the resulting ban lasts, so 4 failures in 5 minutes gets a 2-hour ban, no more and no less than what was asked. And I keep the logpath distro-specific in my head -- Ubuntu's auth.log versus RHEL's secure log -- because getting that wrong means the filter is watching a file that never gets the lines it's looking for, and the jail silently never fires.
questions.example:
# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
[sshd]
enabled  = true
port     = ssh
filter   = sshd
logpath  = /var/log/auth.log
maxretry = 4
findtime = 5m
bantime  = 2h

# Check current bans:
fail2ban-client status sshd

# Unban a specific IP immediately:
fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 203.0.113.42
commonMistakes: Editing jail.conf directly instead of jail.local, so the change disappears on the next package upgrade
Using the RHEL/CentOS logpath (/var/log/secure) on an Ubuntu box instead of /var/log/auth.log
Swapping maxretry and findtime's meanings, or getting bantime's unit wrong
Forgetting fail2ban watches log files, not live network traffic, when explaining how the jail actually detects the pattern
keyPoints: jail.local overrides jail.conf and survives upgrades
Correct logpath for Ubuntu (/var/log/auth.log)
maxretry/findtime/bantime values matching the prompt exactly
Correct status and unban commands

Correct logpath for Ubuntu specifically

questions.title: Write a Least-Privilege IAM Policy for a Read-Only Archive Bucket
questions.prompt: Write an IAM policy document that grants read-only access (GetObject and ListBucket only) to a single S3 bucket named 'ltv-audit-logs', and requires the caller to have authenticated with MFA. Do not use any wildcard in Action or Resource.
questions.modelAnswer: The policy needs an explicit Action list containing exactly s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket -- never s3:* -- and a Resource list containing two separate ARNs, because the two actions need different ARN shapes: ListBucket operates on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::ltv-audit-logs), while GetObject operates on objects inside it (arn:aws:s3:::ltv-audit-logs/*). A Condition block with Bool and the key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to "true" ties the whole grant to an MFA-authenticated session, so the permissions simply don't apply to a request that hasn't gone through MFA.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail people miss most often here is that ListBucket and GetObject need two different ARN shapes in the Resource array, not one -- ListBucket is a bucket-level operation so it needs the bare bucket ARN, while GetObject reaches into objects so it needs the /* suffix. If you only include one of the two ARNs, one of the two actions silently never actually works even though the policy looks complete. I also never reach for s3:* out of convenience here, because the prompt asked for read-only and a wildcard grants every current and future S3 action automatically, including ones like PutBucketPolicy that have nothing to do with read access. The MFA condition is the last piece -- Bool, aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, "true" -- and it's additive, it only ever narrows the grant further, never widens it.
commonMistakes: Using "s3:*" instead of the two explicit actions actually required
Including only the bucket ARN or only the bucket/* ARN instead of both, silently breaking one of the two actions
Using "Resource": "*" instead of scoping to this one bucket
Omitting the MFA condition, or using the wrong condition operator/key
keyPoints: Explicit Action list with exactly the two needed actions
Both ARN shapes present: the bucket ARN and the bucket/* object ARN
Condition Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent true
No wildcards anywhere in Action or Resource

Correct two-ARN Resource pattern
Correct MFA condition block
No wildcards used anywhere in the policy

questions.title: Write a Bucket Policy That Rejects Plain HTTP
questions.prompt: Your S3 bucket is encrypted at rest, but a teammate points out it will still answer a plain HTTP request. Write the bucket policy statement that denies any request to this bucket that isn't made over TLS.
questions.modelAnswer: This has to be an explicit Deny statement, not just an Allow for HTTPS traffic, because an Allow only grants a permission -- it never closes off whatever else a broader Allow statement elsewhere might already permit. The statement applies to Principal "*" (everyone, since this should hold for any caller), Action "s3:*" (the restriction should apply to every operation against the bucket, not just reads), and both the bucket and bucket/* ARNs. The Condition uses Bool with the key aws:SecureTransport set to "false" -- meaning the Deny fires specifically when the connection was not made over TLS.
questions.professionalAnswer: The instinct a lot of people have is to write an Allow statement requiring SecureTransport true, but that doesn't actually fix anything on its own -- it's additive, and it does nothing to override some other, broader Allow that might already be sitting in the same policy or an attached IAM policy. The fix has to be an explicit Deny, because explicit Deny always wins evaluation regardless of what else matches. I scope the Deny to s3:* rather than just GetObject, because the whole point is that no operation against this bucket should ever be allowed over plain HTTP, not just reads. And I always cover both ARN shapes, the bucket itself and the bucket/* wildcard for objects, the same reason as any S3 policy -- miss one and some subset of calls slip past the restriction.
commonMistakes: Writing an Allow statement for HTTPS instead of an explicit Deny on plain HTTP, which doesn't actually block anything
Scoping the Deny to only one action (like GetObject) instead of s3:*, leaving other operations unprotected
Forgetting to include both the bucket ARN and the bucket/* ARN
Assuming encryption at rest already implies this protection, when it's a completely separate, independently configured setting
keyPoints: Explicit Deny, not an Allow, is required here
aws:SecureTransport condition key checked against "false"
Scoped to s3:* so every operation is covered, not just reads
Both bucket and bucket/* ARNs included

Correct condition key and value
Correct resource coverage (both ARN shapes)

questions.title: Write a Python Function That Pages Through an API With Rate-Limit Backoff
questions.prompt: Write a Python function using the requests library that pages through a threat-intel API's /indicators endpoint using a next_page_token field, and handles HTTP 429 responses with exponential backoff that respects a Retry-After header when present.
questions.modelAnswer: The function needs two things happening at once inside the same loop: pagination and rate-limit handling. Pagination means calling the endpoint, collecting results, checking the response for a next_page_token, and if present, passing it back in on the next request -- stopping only when that field is missing. Rate-limit handling means checking the status code before trusting the response: on a 429, read the Retry-After header if the API provided one and sleep for that long, otherwise fall back to a doubling delay (1s, 2s, 4s...), then retry the same request rather than moving on. A timeout should be set on every request so a hung connection can't stall the script indefinitely, and the real data-collection logic only runs once a non-429 response comes back.
questions.professionalAnswer: The bug I watch for here is a script that pages correctly but has absolutely no 429 handling, so the first time the API throttles it, the function either crashes or -- worse -- just keeps hammering the endpoint and gets the API key throttled further or revoked. I structure this as a retry loop around each individual page request: if the response is 429, I check for Retry-After first because the server knows its own limits better than I'm going to guess, and only fall back to my own doubling delay if that header isn't there. Once a request actually succeeds, I extend my results list and check for next_page_token the normal way. I also never skip the timeout argument -- a request with no timeout can hang forever on a flaky connection, and that's a much quieter failure than a 429 because nothing ever comes back to tell you it's stuck.
questions.example:
import time
import requests

def get_all_indicators_with_backoff(base_url, headers, max_retries=5):
    all_items = []
    params = {"page_size": 100}
    while True:
        delay = 1
        for attempt in range(max_retries):
            response = requests.get(base_url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=10)
            if response.status_code == 429:
                retry_after = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", delay))
                time.sleep(retry_after)
                delay *= 2
                continue
            response.raise_for_status()
            payload = response.json()
            break
        else:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Exceeded {max_retries} retries against {base_url}")

        all_items.extend(payload["results"])
        next_token = payload.get("next_page_token")
        if not next_token:
            break
        params["page_token"] = next_token

    return all_items
commonMistakes: Looping on next_page_token with no handling at all for a 429 response
Retrying immediately on a 429 instead of backing off, risking further throttling or key revocation
Ignoring the Retry-After header when the API actually provides one, instead of always guessing a fixed delay
Omitting timeout= on the request, risking an indefinite hang on a stalled connection
keyPoints: Pagination loop that continues until next_page_token is absent
429 detection before treating any response as successful
Retry-After respected when present; exponential doubling as the fallback
Explicit timeout set on every request

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct pagination loop logic
Correct 429 detection and backoff handling
Respects Retry-After when the API provides it

questions.title: Write an Azure NSG Rule and Explain What Happens to the Reply Traffic
questions.prompt: Write the az network nsg rule create command that allows inbound HTTPS (443) traffic from the internet to a web subnet's NSG, with a priority that guarantees it's evaluated before the built-in default rules. Then explain, without writing another rule, why you don't need to write a separate rule to let the response traffic back out.
questions.modelAnswer: The command needs --direction Inbound, --access Allow, --protocol Tcp, a source of Internet, and --destination-port-ranges 443, with a --priority well below the 65000-65500 range the undeletable default rules occupy, since Azure evaluates rules in priority order (lower first) and stops at the first match. Because NSGs are stateful, once this rule permits an inbound connection on 443, the NSG automatically recognizes and permits the matching reply traffic going back out -- there's no need to write a mirrored outbound rule, because the firewall isn't evaluating that reply packet against the rule set from scratch, it's recognizing it as part of a connection it already approved.
questions.professionalAnswer: Priority is the field people get wrong most often -- pick something like 100, well under 4096, and definitely nowhere near the 65000+ range where the undeletable default rules live, because if you accidentally land in or above that range your rule either doesn't take priority the way you intended or doesn't matter at all since a default rule already matched first. Once the inbound Allow is in place, I don't write anything for the return path, because NSGs track connection state the same way a stateful firewall does -- the reply to a connection the NSG already approved just rides back out automatically. If someone on the team starts writing a matching outbound rule for the reply traffic, that's the tell they're thinking about this as a stateless device, which an NSG isn't.
questions.example:
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-prod \
  --nsg-name nsg-web-subnet \
  --name Allow-HTTPS-Inbound \
  --priority 100 \
  --direction Inbound \
  --access Allow \
  --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes Internet \
  --destination-port-ranges 443
commonMistakes: Choosing a priority number in or near the 65000+ range, putting the rule after the undeletable default rules
Forgetting --direction Inbound or using the wrong access value
Writing an unnecessary mirrored outbound rule for the reply traffic, as if the NSG were stateless
keyPoints: Priority must be well below the 65000+ default-rule range to take precedence
Correct direction/access/protocol/port fields
NSGs are stateful; reply traffic to an approved inbound connection is automatically permitted

Correct direction/protocol/port fields

questions.title: Write an AWS Security Group Rule, Then the NACL Entry an SG Can't Express
questions.prompt: Write the AWS CLI command to allow inbound HTTPS (443) from anywhere on a given Security Group. Then, separately, write the Network ACL entry you'd use if you needed to explicitly deny traffic from a known-bad /24 range at the subnet level -- something the Security Group alone cannot express.
questions.modelAnswer: The Security Group rule uses aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress with the target group ID, protocol tcp, port 443, and a 0.0.0.0/0 CIDR -- notice there's no priority field and no way to specify Deny, because a Security Group can only ever express Allow; every SG starts from an implicit deny-all and rules are additive. To explicitly deny a known-bad range, that has to be a Network ACL entry instead, using aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry with a numbered rule and --rule-action deny, attached at the subnet level. NACLs support explicit Allow and Deny and evaluate rules in numbered order (lowest first, first match wins), but they are stateless, so a deny on inbound traffic from that range doesn't need, and doesn't get, an automatic outbound equivalent.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always clarify first is that there's no version of this where you add a 'deny' rule to the Security Group itself -- that's not a syntax you're missing, it's a capability Security Groups simply don't have. If a design genuinely needs to block a known-bad range at the network layer, that has to move to a Network ACL, which is the subnet-level, stateless construct that actually supports explicit Deny alongside Allow, evaluated in rule-number order. The stateless part matters operationally too -- unlike the SG, which is stateful and needs no return-traffic rule, a NACL deny on inbound doesn't automatically protect or need anything symmetrical on the outbound side, because NACLs don't track connections at all.
questions.example:
# Security Group: allow inbound HTTPS from anywhere
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-0abc123def456 \
  --protocol tcp \
  --port 443 \
  --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# NACL: explicitly deny a known-bad /24 at the subnet level
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-0123abcd \
  --ingress \
  --rule-number 50 \
  --protocol -1 \
  --cidr-block 198.51.100.0/24 \
  --rule-action deny
commonMistakes: Trying to write a Deny rule directly on the Security Group, which isn't possible -- SGs are allow-only
Forgetting NACLs are stateless, unlike Security Groups, so return traffic isn't automatically handled
Giving the NACL entry a rule number that doesn't reflect intended evaluation order (lowest number evaluated first)
keyPoints: Security Groups are allow-only and implicitly deny everything else by default
Correct SG ingress CLI command
NACL as the correct construct for an explicit subnet-level Deny
NACLs are stateless, unlike the stateful Security Group

Correct NACL deny entry
Correctly notes NACL statelessness vs. SG statefulness

questions.title: Wire SAST and Dependency Scanning Into a CI Pipeline
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow step sequence for a Python project that runs on every pull request: install dependencies, run Bandit as a SAST check, and run pip-audit as a dependency scan -- both before the application is ever built into a deployable artifact.
questions.modelAnswer: The workflow needs to trigger on pull_request so the checks run on every incoming change, not just on merges to main. After checking out the code and setting up Python with actions/setup-python, dependencies install from requirements.txt. The SAST step installs and runs Bandit recursively against the source directory; the dependency-scan step installs and runs pip-audit against the same requirements file. Both run before any build/package/deploy step, because they're the cheapest, fastest checks in the pipeline and should catch problems as early as possible rather than after time has already been spent building an artifact.
questions.professionalAnswer: The ordering in this workflow is the actual point, not just which tools are listed. Both Bandit and pip-audit can run in seconds against a diff with no running application and no test environment, which is exactly why they belong on every single pull request rather than a nightly build -- the whole value of shift-left security is catching cheap, fast findings before anyone has sunk time into a build. I always trigger on pull_request specifically, not push to main, because the point is to catch this before the change merges, not after. If I saw these two scans running after a 'build and deploy' step in someone's workflow, that tells me they understand what the tools do but not why the order actually matters.
questions.example:
name: build-and-scan
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Run SAST (Bandit)
        run: pip install bandit && bandit -r src/ -f json -o bandit-report.json
      - name: Run dependency scan (pip-audit)
        run: pip install pip-audit && pip-audit -r requirements.txt
commonMistakes: Running the scans after the build/deploy step instead of before it, losing the fast-feedback benefit
Triggering only on push to main instead of on every pull request
Forgetting to install Bandit and pip-audit explicitly in the workflow before invoking them
Omitting actions/setup-python, leaving the Python version ambiguous and inconsistent
keyPoints: Trigger on pull_request, not just push to main
actions/setup-python with an explicit version, then install requirements
Bandit run recursively against the source directory
pip-audit run against requirements.txt, both steps before any build step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct trigger and setup steps
Correct Bandit (SAST) step
Correct pip-audit (SCA) step
Correctly places both before the build step, with reasoning

questions.title: Write a Basic KQL Query to Pull One User's Failed Sign-Ins
questions.prompt: Write a KQL query against SigninLogs that returns only the UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, and ResultType columns for failed sign-ins (ResultType != "0") belonging to a specific user, 'j.martinez@contoso.com', sorted by most recent first.
questions.modelAnswer: The query starts with the SigninLogs table and pipes through filters in the order they're written, since KQL's written order is its execution order. A 'where' clause filters to the specific user, a second 'where' filters to failures only (ResultType != "0" -- comparisons are case-sensitive in KQL, and ResultType is stored as a string, not a number), 'project' narrows to just the three requested columns, and 'sort by TimeGenerated desc' orders the result most-recent-first.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a case where getting the structure exactly right matters more than the query being clever -- it's just SigninLogs piped through two where clauses, a project, and a sort. The detail I'd flag to a newer analyst is that ResultType is compared as a string, "0", not the number 0, and KQL string comparisons are case-sensitive by default, so == and != behave exactly as written with no implicit type coercion the way some other query languages might do. I also default to 'sort by ... desc' rather than assuming the table is already ordered by time -- SigninLogs isn't guaranteed to come back in any particular order unless you ask for it.
questions.example:
SigninLogs
| where UserPrincipalName == "j.martinez@contoso.com"
| where ResultType != "0"
| project UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, ResultType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
commonMistakes: Writing SQL-style SELECT...FROM...WHERE syntax instead of KQL's piped table-then-operators order
Comparing ResultType as a number instead of the string "0"
Forgetting KQL string comparisons are case-sensitive by default
Omitting desc, returning the oldest sign-ins first instead of most recent
keyPoints: Table name first, then piped operators in execution order
Correct != "0" string comparison for failures
project to the three requested columns only
sort by TimeGenerated desc for most-recent-first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct table/pipe structure
Correct filter syntax for the user and failure condition
Correct project with exactly the requested columns
Correct sort direction

questions.title: Write the Conditional Access Policy Pieces for a Finance Group
questions.prompt: Write out the four pieces (assignments, conditions, grant controls, session controls) of a Conditional Access policy that requires the Finance security group to use MFA and sign in from a compliant device, and make sure your answer explicitly accounts for the break-glass accounts.
questions.modelAnswer: Assignments: target the Finance security group specifically, and explicitly exclude the organization's break-glass emergency-access accounts from this policy -- that exclusion is not optional, since a policy with no path around it for an emergency account is exactly what locks out an admin during an outage. Conditions: all cloud apps the Finance team actually uses (or all cloud apps, if the org wants this broadly applied). Grant controls: require both MFA and a compliant device, selecting 'require all the selected controls' rather than 'require one of,' since the requirement is both, not either. Session controls: optionally, a sign-in frequency control to re-prompt periodically rather than trusting a single login indefinitely. Before switching this policy to 'On,' it should run in report-only mode against real sign-ins to confirm it resolves the way intended, including for any service accounts or off-hours access in the Finance group.
questions.professionalAnswer: The piece I'd never skip, even under time pressure, is the break-glass exclusion in the Assignments section -- that's the single most damaging Conditional Access mistake, a policy that can block the very admin accounts needed to fix it if something goes wrong. For the Grant controls, I'm deliberate about choosing 'require all' rather than 'require one of,' because the actual requirement here is MFA and a compliant device together, not either one alone satisfying the policy. And I never flip a new policy straight to 'On' -- I run it in report-only first against real sign-in logs long enough to see how it resolves for real traffic patterns, including anything unusual like off-hours access, before trusting it to actually enforce.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to explicitly exclude break-glass accounts from the policy's assignments
Selecting 'require one of' when both MFA and compliant device were actually required together
Switching the policy straight to 'On' without first validating it in report-only mode
Scoping assignments to 'All users' instead of the specific Finance group the requirement was about
keyPoints: All four pieces (assignments, conditions, grant controls, session controls) addressed
Explicit break-glass account exclusion in assignments
Grant controls set to require all, not require one of
Report-only validation mentioned before enforcement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines assignments including the break-glass exclusion
Correct conditions
Correct grant-control logic (require all, not one of)
Mentions report-only validation before enabling

questions.title: A Burst of Event ID 4625 Against One Account
questions.prompt: Your SIEM fires an alert: 40 Event ID 4625 entries against the same account in the last 10 minutes, originating from 6 different source machines. Walk through what this pattern most likely indicates, and what you'd check next before declaring it a confirmed incident.
questions.modelAnswer: A burst of 4625 (failed logon) events against one account is the signature of a password-guessing or brute-force attempt -- a single mistyped password doesn't produce 40 failures, and the fact that these failures are coming from 6 different source machines rather than one points toward an automated or distributed attempt rather than one person struggling to type their own password. Before declaring this confirmed, I'd check whether any of those attempts, or any attempt shortly after this burst, actually succeeded -- correlating against a 4624 for the same account in the same window is the single most important next step, since a burst that never succeeds is a different severity than one that ends in a successful logon. I'd also check whether other accounts show the same multi-source failure pattern around the same time, which would reframe this as password spraying against many accounts rather than brute-forcing one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing that pattern tells me is that this isn't a 'someone forgot their password' story -- 40 failures from 6 different machines in 10 minutes doesn't happen by accident. But I don't jump straight to 'confirmed incident' off the burst alone; the next thing I pull is whether a 4624 success shows up for this same account right after or during that window, because that single fact changes everything about the severity and the response. I'd also check whether this is isolated to one account or whether other accounts in the environment show the same multi-source failure signature at the same time, since that distinguishes a targeted brute-force attempt from a broader password-spraying campaign, and those two get handled differently.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is just a user mistyping their password without checking whether any attempt ultimately succeeded
Treating single-machine and multi-machine failure bursts as the same pattern, when multi-source strongly suggests automation
Not checking whether other accounts show the same pattern, which would point to password spraying rather than a single-account brute force
keyPoints: 4625 bursts are the brute-force/credential-guessing signature
Multi-source failures suggest automation, not a single human mistake
Correlating against a 4624 success for the same account is the critical next check
Checking other accounts for the same pattern distinguishes brute force from spraying

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the pattern as a credential attack
Identifies checking for a subsequent success as the critical next step
Considers the spraying-vs-brute-force distinction
Correctly scopes other reasonable next steps
